prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This synod is convinced that the forces of the Allies are being used of God to vindicate the rights of the weak and to maintain the moral order of the world. Anglican Synod, Melbourne, 1916. Bit weird at first, That starey look in the eyes, The hair down past his shoulders, But after a go with the ship’s barber, A sea-water shower and the old slouch hat Across his ears, he started to look the part. Took him a while to get the way A bayonet fits the old Lee-Enfield, But going in on the boats He looked calmer than any of us, Just gazing in over the swell Where the cliffs looked black against the sky. When we hit he fairly raced in through the waves, Then up the beach, swerving like a full-back at the end When the Turks’d really got on to us. Time we all caught up, He was off like a flash, up the cliffs, After his first machine gun. He’d done for three Turks when we got there, The fourth was a gibbering mess. Seeing him wave that blood-red bayonet, I reckoned we were glad To have him on the side.

outputs.L1:
“This synod is convinced that the forces of the Allies are being used of God to vindicate the rights of the weak and to maintain the moral order of the world.”  
—Anglican Synod, Melbourne, 1916

Bit weird at first—  
that starey look in the eyes,  
the hair down past his shoulders.  
But after a go with the ship’s barber,  
a sea-water shower, and the old slouch hat  
across his ears, he started to look the part.

Took him a while to get the way  
a bayonet fits the old Lee-Enfield,  
but going in on the boats,  
he looked calmer than any of us—  
just gazing in over the swell,  
where the cliffs looked black against the sky.

When we hit, he fairly raced in through the waves,  
then up the beach, swerving like a full-back at the end,  
when the Turks’d really got on to us.  
By the time we all caught up,  
he was off like a flash, up the cliffs,  
after his first machine gun.

He’d done for three Turks when we got there;  
the fourth was a gibbering mess.  
Seeing him wave that blood-red bayonet,  
I reckoned we were glad  
to have him on the side.
outputs.L2:
The synod believes that God is working through the Allied forces to defend the rights of the vulnerable and preserve the world’s moral order.  
—Anglican Synod, Melbourne, 1916

At first, he seemed an odd figure—  
eyes fixed in an unsettling gaze,  
hair hanging below his shoulders.  
But once the ship’s barber had attended to him,  
he had washed in seawater,  
and an old slouch hat had been pulled down over his ears,  
he began to resemble one of us.

It took some time for him to learn  
how the bayonet fastened onto an old Lee-Enfield.  
Yet as the boats carried us in,  
he appeared more composed than anyone else,  
silently watching beyond the rolling water  
toward the cliffs, dark against the sky.

The moment we landed, he charged through the surf  
and sprinted across the shore,  
dodging from side to side like a full-back near the finish,  
just as the Turks began to find their range.

By the time the rest of us reached him,  
he had already shot up the cliffs  
in pursuit of his first machine gun.  
When we arrived, three Turks were dead,  
and a fourth had been reduced to terrified babbling.

As he brandished the bayonet, now bright red with blood,  
I remember thinking how fortunate we were  
that he was fighting on our side.
outputs.L3:
The Anglican Synod presents the Allied war effort as a sacred mission, declaring that the soldiers are serving God by protecting the weak and preserving the world’s moral order. This religious endorsement gives the conflict an appearance of righteousness, suggesting that military violence is justified because it is carried out in defence of supposedly Christian values.

The sequence then introduces a strange-looking, long-haired recruit whose appearance evokes traditional images of Christ. He is groomed, dressed in uniform, and issued military equipment until his individuality is erased and he resembles a conventional Australian soldier. Although he is initially unfamiliar with his rifle and bayonet, he remains remarkably calm as the troops approach the battlefield.

Once ashore, however, the recruit undergoes a disturbing transformation. He charges through enemy fire and kills several Turkish soldiers with shocking speed and efficiency. The contrast between his Christ-like appearance and his brutal actions creates a powerful irony. By turning a figure associated with peace, mercy, and sacrifice into an effective killer, the sequence exposes the troubling way religious language and imagery can be used to sanctify warfare and justify violence.
outputs.L4:
The poem offers a powerful critique of the religious language used to justify Allied violence during the First World War. At its centre is a Christ-like recruit who is transformed into an Australian soldier fighting at Gallipoli. Traditionally, Christ represents mercy, sacrifice, forgiveness, and love for one’s enemies. In the poem, however, these qualities are displaced by the values demanded of a successful combatant: obedience, aggression, endurance, and the ability to kill. The transformation therefore exposes the deep contradiction between Christian teaching and modern warfare.

The soldier’s brutal effectiveness is central to the poem’s irony. Rather than behaving as the biblical Christ would, he proves himself through violence and becomes useful to the military because he can destroy the enemy. His success may appear heroic within the values of wartime patriotism, but it also reveals how completely those values have distorted the religious figure on whom they claim to rely. The poem suggests that a nation cannot plausibly invoke Christ as its supporter while celebrating actions that oppose his teachings.

By placing this figure at Gallipoli, the poem also challenges heroic accounts of Australian military identity. Gallipoli is often associated with courage, sacrifice, comradeship, and the birth of national consciousness, yet the poem draws attention to the violence beneath those ideals. The Christ-like soldier does not sanctify the campaign; instead, the campaign degrades and militarises Christ. Sacred authority is appropriated to make killing appear righteous, while religious faith is reshaped to serve nationalism and military power.

Ultimately, the poem does not merely question whether God is on the Allied side. It condemns the broader attempt to claim divine approval for war. Through bitter irony, it shows that militarism corrupts both faith and moral judgement: Christ can accompany the army only after being remade in the army’s image. The resulting figure embodies not Christian redemption but the destructive values of war, revealing the hypocrisy of using religion to legitimise organised violence.

**This, Allies, God**

This is the moment when courage matters most. We may face uncertainty, but we do not face it alone. Our allies stand beside us, offering strength, wisdom, and hope. Above all, faith in God reminds us that even the hardest journey can have meaning. United by trust and guided by compassion, we can move forward together.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem imagining Jesus as an Australian soldier landing at Gallipoli, preceded by a 1916 quotation from the Anglican Synod in Melbourne about the Allies serving God.
counterfactuals.output:
> “The Allies are fighting in the service of God.”  
> —Anglican Synod of Melbourne, 1916

**Ninth Hour at Anzac**

He comes ashore before sunrise,  
khaki dark with salt,  
a slouch hat pulled low  
over the old wound of heaven.

No donkey waits—  
only the crush of boats,  
the clatter of rifles,  
men spilling into water  
red as a psalm no chaplain dare read aloud.

Jesus carries a Lee–Enfield  
but will not fire.

He shoulders instead  
a boy from Ballarat  
whose mouth keeps making  
the shape of *Mum*.

Up the impossible ridge  
the officers cry,  
Forward—

and the guns answer  
from scrub and stone.

At Shrapnel Gully  
he tears his puttees into bandages.  
At Quinn’s Post  
he gives his water away.  
By noon he has died  
in several accents:

Irish,  
Turkish,  
Arabic,  
the broad bush vowels  
of New South Wales.

Each time he rises  
only far enough  
to reach the next wounded man.

The Synod says God  
has chosen a side.

But here God lies  
between the trenches,  
face pressed into foreign thyme,  
one hand stretched toward the Empire,  
one toward the Turk,

and both hands empty.

At dusk they find him  
caught on the wire,  
his arms spread wide  
as if the hill itself  
had built a cross.

No one knows  
which uniform to bury him in.

The sea keeps breathing below.  
The stars come out  
over Gallipoli—

indifferent, innumerable—

and all night long  
the dead of both armies  
hear him whisper:

Forgive them.

They have mistaken  
their flags  
for the kingdom of heaven.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a satirical anti-war poem in the voice of an ANZAC infantryman who describes Christ joining his unit, being given a haircut, slouch hat, Lee-Enfield rifle, and bayonet, then charging Turkish positions.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The New Recruit**

They sent us Christ at break of day,  
No thunderclap, no choir—  
Just dusty feet and wounded hands  
Beside the cookhouse fire.  
The sergeant said, “You’ll never pass  
With hair like that, my son,”  
And clipped His curls with army shears  
To Regulation One.

We jammed a slouch hat on His head,  
Turned up the proper side,  
Then gave Him boots, a khaki coat,  
And taught Him how to stride.  
A Lee-Enfield filled His hands,  
A bayonet gleamed below;  
“Salvation’s good,” the corporal said,  
“But steel’s the go, you know.”

He asked us who the Turks had wronged.  
We said we couldn’t say.  
The papers called them devils, though,  
So devils they must stay.  
He asked what hill we meant to win,  
What kingdom waited there.  
The major pointed with his stick:  
“Advance, and don’t ask where.”

At dawn we climbed from out the trench,  
Christ charging with the rest,  
His rifle held across His ribs,  
His slouch hat on His breast.  
The Turkish guns began to preach,  
And shells pronounced their creed;  
While generals, safe behind the ridge,  
Put God to splendid use indeed.

He reached the wire and saw beyond  
A frightened Turkish lad,  
Who wore the same bewildered look  
That every soldier had.  
Christ dropped His blade. The Turk dropped his.  
They stared across the din—  
Till both sides’ righteous officers  
Cried, “That’s no way to win!”

A bullet found the Saviour then—  
Whose, no one cared to tell.  
We dragged Him down through dust and blood  
And laid Him where He fell.  
The chaplain said, “God’s on our side,”  
The imam said the same;  
And Christ, between their certainties,  
Asked neither man his name.

Next morning came the casualty list,  
Correct in every part:  
“One private, killed while charging—  
Gunshot wound through heart.”  
The colonel praised His sacrifice,  
The press declared it grand;  
And somewhere men made medals  
While the dead reclaimed the land.

So if He comes again, old mate,  
With peace upon His tongue,  
Hide Him from the barber’s chair,  
And keep Him ever young.  
For armies welcome Prince and God,  
Then drill them, file them, feed—  
And issue Christ a bayonet  
To save the world with greed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a historically grounded dramatic monologue about a long-haired, Christ-like recruit at Gallipoli. Use colloquial Australian language, vivid landing imagery, and an ironic epigraph showing church support for World War I.
counterfactuals.output:
> *“To save the freedom of the world and to save Liberty’s own self… to kill Germans—not for the sake of killing, but to save the world.”*  
> —Arthur Winnington-Ingram, Bishop of London, wartime sermon, 1915

They called him Jesus from the minute he came aboard—  
not in the prayer-book way, mind. We were Australians.  
We’d nickname the Almighty “Bluey” if He had red hair.

The lad’s name was Eli Mercer. Nineteen, maybe twenty,  
skinny as a tent peg, with brown hair to his shoulders  
and a little fork of beard the sergeant hated on sight.

“Get that scrub sheared off,” he says.

Eli only smiles. “Samson lost his strength that way, Sarge.”

That earned him pack drill—and the name stuck.

He’d been a carpenter, too. Fair dinkum.  
Could mend a crate, shape a wedge, set a splint.  
On the troopship he fixed a padre’s folding altar  
after the sea kicked it flat. The padre said,  
“God has given you a useful gift, son.”

Funny thing to say to a bloke bound for Gallipoli.

Before dawn on the twenty-fifth, we climbed down  
from the destroyer into those little pulling boats,  
rifles knocking knees, packs dragging at our shoulders.  
The Aegean looked black and oily. You could smell  
salt, wet rope, sweat, and the bully beef we’d spewed up.  
Nobody sang then. Not “Australia Will Be There,”  
not “Onward, Christian Soldiers.” We’d sung ourselves empty  
between Egypt and the island.

Ahead was a smudge of land. Ari Burnu.  
Not the broad, easy beach the maps had promised,  
but shingle under cliffs, gullies snarled with thorn,  
ridges piled one behind another like the backs  
of crouching beasts.

Then the rifles began.

Little flashes winked in the dark above us.  
The water snapped—tick, tick, tick—  
as if God Almighty had thrown a fistful of gravel.  
One chap pitched over the gunwale without a word.  
Another cried for his mum. The naval bloke steering us  
said, “Sit down, you silly bastards,” very calm,  
as though we were skylarking on the Yarra.

When the keel grated, we jumped.

Cold water to the waist. Boots sinking.  
A pack could drown you quicker than any Turk,  
so blokes went ashore clawing off straps,  
rifles held high like candles in a procession.  
The beach was all white stones, black blood,  
and men trying to make themselves smaller.

Eli stood up.

I yelled, “Get down, Jesus!”

He turned, hair plastered round his face,  
and for half a second—dawn coming red behind him,  
arms spread to balance in the surf—  
he looked like the picture over my mother’s bed.

Then he bent and lifted young Davo Collins,  
who’d caught one through the thigh.

“Leave him!” I shouted. “We’ve got to push on!”

Eli said, “You push on, then.”

No sermon. No heavenly choir. Just that.

He carried Davo over the stones while the shrapnel  
burst above us in dirty yellow puffs. The pellets came down  
hissing through the scrub. The wounded lay calling  
for stretcher-bearers, water, mothers, Christ—  
anyone who might still be listening.

We climbed towards Plugge’s Plateau, slipping in dust,  
bayonets catching in holly oak and prickly scrub.  
Officers waved revolvers and vanished into gullies.  
Units mixed together—Victorians, Queenslanders,  
New South Welshmen—every man asking where the line was,  
when there wasn’t any bloody line. Only uphill,  
and bullets coming downhill.

Eli kept appearing among us. Binding a hand.  
Giving away his water. Dragging a bloke behind a rock.  
Once I saw him kneeling over a Turk no older than him,  
holding the enemy lad’s wrist as if feeling for a pulse.

“What are you doing?” I said.

“He’s dying.”

“He’s a Turk.”

“Not for much longer.”

That was Eli: cheeky to sergeants, gentle with the dead,  
and no more use to an empire than mercy ever is.

He copped it near evening, below Baby 700.  
A machine-gun swept the slope. We all went flat,  
faces in thyme and dust. When it stopped,  
Eli was sitting against a bank, looking surprised.  
There was a dark hole under his ribs.

The padre found us after sunset.  
He’d lost his altar somewhere on the beach.

He said, “Tell him his sacrifice is sacred.”

Eli laughed—just one little breath.

“Sacrifice?” he says. “Who asked me?”

Then he took my hand. His palm was rough  
from timber, though the nails were clean.  
Above us the warships fired, great orange mouths  
opening on the sea, and the shells passed overhead  
with the sound of whole churches being torn from their foundations.

“Don’t let them make it pretty, mate,” he said.

So I won’t.

He died in the dirt with his long hair full of burrs.  
No cross, except the rifle laid beside him.  
No resurrection, except Davo Collins lived  
to limp round Ballarat for another forty years.

And on Sunday, they tell me, the bishops rang the bells  
and called the slaughter holy.

Well—good on them.

From where we stood at Gallipoli,  
heaven was very loud,  
and no bugger came down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem critiquing the fusion of Christianity, nationalism, and military violence during the First World War. Contrast an official Anglican Synod statement with a soldier’s casual account of Jesus killing enemy troops.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Minutes of the Kingdom**

The Synod met beneath carved saints  
and windows red with martyrdom.  
It blessed the “righteous cause,” declared  
the nation’s sword an instrument  
of Providence—  
each regiment a psalm in khaki,  
each gun obedient to God.

The bishops’ sentences marched well:  
*Justice, sacrifice, holy duty;*  
England folded into Christ  
until the flag became a cross  
and the cross acquired a bayonet.

Later, in a letter from the mud,  
a soldier wrote without theology:  
“Jesus was with us yesterday—  
helped us kill a lot of Huns.”

No creed. No careful clause.  
Only a cigarette’s shrug  
between barrage and breakfast,  
as though the Prince of Peace had stooped  
to feed the Maxim gun.

Perhaps that was the Synod’s faith  
translated faithfully:  
incense into cordite,  
anthem into shell-fire,  
the Lamb of God made lion,  
then made nation,  
then made aim.

Across the wire, another chaplain  
raised the same white hands,  
asked the same Christ  
to guard grey sons from English steel.

And heaven, requisitioned twice,  
hung silent over Flanders  
while Christians killed Christians  
for Christian kings—

each bullet stamped with Caesar,  
each grave marked with a cross.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a darkly ironic Australian war poem in which the narrator initially finds Jesus strange but comes to admire him after he storms the cliffs and attacks a Turkish machine-gun crew with a blood-red bayonet.
counterfactuals.output:
### **A New Gospel at the Narrows**

I never took to Jesus much—  
too pale, too clean, too mild;  
a plaster bloke in Sunday robes,  
all lamb and little child.  
He looked no use at Anzac Cove,  
where God had lost the map,  
and Turkish guns stitched scarlet seams  
through every slouch-hat chap.

But dawn came hard upon the cliffs,  
a brass and bloody sun,  
and there he stood beside us  
when the climbing had begun.  
No halo—just a sweat-stained shirt,  
no sermon, hymn, or prayer;  
he swore beneath his breath like us  
and fixed his bayonet there.

He stormed the ridge through scrub and smoke,  
past boys who would not rise,  
with shrapnel ringing round his head  
like bells from Paradise.  
The Turkish gun kept hammering;  
its crew worked grim and fast—  
till Jesus vaulted through their trench  
and reached them all at last.

His steel was red as altar wine,  
his hands as red as clay;  
he drove the gunners from their post  
in Heaven’s newest way.  
Then, panting by the silent gun,  
he gave a crooked grin—  
as if to say salvation meant  
you first must charge the sin.

I liked him better after that.  
He seemed an honest sort:  
not much at turning cheeks, perhaps,  
but handy in support.  
The padre said, “He died for peace.”  
We watched the hillside steam—  
and praised the Prince of Peace because  
he’d killed their whole gun team.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
